recZOKCUcQhghoKqF.Name: Kayleigh Berkana

reckIvJxU4wRhybxA.Bio: Mario Garza is the artist and researcher behind Symbolic Studies, a project sharing symbolic insights on the zodiac, mythology, folklore and world religions, with astrology as its foundation. A lifelong artist who has worked as an art director and graphic designer for nearly 25 years, he runs Symbolic Studies from the Pacific Northwest alongside his wife Michelle, who co-hosts the podcast with him. His work traces syncretic threads across tarot, occultism and comparative religion, including the argument that the major deities of antiquity were originally polar gods before a solar model was laid over them. He also offers symbolic birth chart and tarot readings, private lessons and freelance design.
reckIvJxU4wRhybxA.Name: Mario Garza

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Juan Ayala's Portrait of Lovecraft", "body": "Juan Ayala sets the stage by calling Lovecraft one of history's most prolific letter writers, with estimates he puts at 75,000 to 100,000 letters, many as long as books, written by a man Juan describes as a virtual hermit who never really held a job. Juan traces the mythos to a childhood obsession with the Arabian Nights, which he says inspired the alter ego Abdul Alhazred, supposed author of the Necronomicon, and to a grandfather's library said to hold the Picatrix. He names Lovecraft's racism plainly while crediting his reach into films like The Thing and Color Out of Space, plus video, card and board games."}, {"title": "Pluto as Lovecraft's Planet", "body": "Kayleigh Berkana comes at Lovecraft through Pluto, a planet she says astrologers tie to darkness before deep transformation and rebirth. She recounts Percival Lowell's search for a Planet X beyond Neptune and Clyde Tombaugh's discovery on February 18, 1930, noting that Lovecraft, a keen student of astronomy who wrote for journals, lived until 1937, and she places the discovery in Cancer near Ursa Major and Ursa Minor. Gabe says the first recorded hint of Pluto fell on Lovecraft's nineteenth birthday, the panel notes a feature on Pluto named for Cthulhu, and Gabe frames the coming American Pluto return to its 1776 position as the scale of the spell."}, {"title": "How Occultists Adopted the Mythos", "body": "Mario Garza argues that however Lovecraft's work came to be, he was tapped in, updating an older pantheon for modern sensibilities, and that his influence runs through an underground of black magical books and groups. Mario says he found a reverence for the north, the North Star and Ursa Major that goes largely unnoticed, and that some Lovecraftian groups vet initiates by whether their psyche survives a ritual, while others treat the North Star as an astral gateway out and back. Pointing to the steady stream of rituals, spells and new versions of the Necronomicon, he says he doubts people would keep doing this if it did not work."}, {"title": "Fiction, Fear and the Dreaming God", "body": "Gabe floats the theory that the whole Lovecraft web may be the largest black magic LARP of all time, run by masters of fiction, while Chance questions the idea of entities outside reality and frames Mark Passio's notion of cosmic abandonment as a perspective gap that nature's symbolic correspondences can close. The panel turns to Azathoth, the blind idiot god whose dream is said to be our reality, and the conversation reads this as fictionalized pop gnosticism, suggesting that people who crack open expanded consciousness while carrying fear and impurity find that fear amplified back at them."}, {"title": "Taking Back the Power From Fear", "body": "The closing strand turns from horror to agency. Gabe says horror fans tend to adopt a passive posture while he steers his imagination, and he reads the image of Andrew Jackson slaying the many headed bank monster as a way of stirring inherited fears of financial collapse. Kayleigh counters that anyone can read a chart but no chart shows the human soul or its willpower, and Chance closes by arguing that believing in any boogeyman greater than our divine spark only breeds bigger ones, insisting we are the imagination that dreams reality. In a last exchange, the panel weighs Lovecraft's line that fear is the strongest emotion against love."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Get ready to release the Kraken tonight as we crack into the deranged skull of H.P. Lovecraft and decode his C'Thonic mythology, it's cultural influence, astrological significance, and symbolic strangeness. This super-panel live stream starring Slick Dissident (Gabriel), Juan from The Juan on Juan Podcast, Mario Garza from Symbolic Studies, and astrologer Kayleigh Berkana, might just leave you feeling the aybss staring back.
